name: Anaphora Resolution
description: Evaluates the frequency of explicit noun repetition versus the natural use of pronouns (anaphora) for coreference.
mechanism: This method studies how a text handles anaphora—the use of pronouns (e.g., 'it', 'they', 'she') to refer back to previously established nouns. Humans unconsciously rely heavily on anaphora because our cognitive context smoothly carries the reference forward, preventing redundant wordiness. However, LLMs (due to their self-attention mechanisms and reinforced safety training focused on absolute, unambiguous clarity) often exhibit 'anaphora avoidance'. They have a statistically higher tendency to explicitly repeat the core noun ('The company announced...', 'The company stated...', 'The company\'s goal...') instead of using pronouns. By tracking the ratio of explicit coreferences to anaphoric pronouns, this system exposes the overly-cautious structural scaffolding typical of machine generation.
useCase: Detecting text generated by LLMs that prioritize absolute sentence-level clarity and neutrality by avoiding natural human pronoun usage.
strengths:
• Targets the fundamental self-attention nature of transformer models, which weigh explicit nouns higher for context retention.
• Highly effective on narrative, informative, and summarization texts.
• Subtle enough that standard humanizing prompts fail to bypass it without breaking text cohesion.
limitations:
• Susceptible to false positives when human writers draft legal, highly formal, or academic documents that intentionally avoid ambiguity.
• Requires heavy NLP coreference resolution models for accurate entity mapping.
• Performance drops significantly on very short texts where coreference chains cannot form.
parameters:
Analysis: Syntactic Coreference Tracking
Metric: Explicit Noun vs. Pronoun Ratio
Output: 0-100 Anaphora Avoidance Score
accuracy: Moderate to High — 76-82%. Very effective in identifying 'corporate style' or overly formal AI summaries.

references.title: Manning, C.D. & Schütze, H. (1999). Foundations of Statistical Natural Language Processing. MIT Press.
